conceptTag: How many coffees does your city drink a day?
readerTitle: How many coffees does your city drink a day? A napkin can tell you
caseNote: 가상 사례 (두 번째 매장을 고민하는 카페 주인, 종이컵 도매업체) · 모든 수치는 설명용 가정
insight: 모르는 큰 숫자도 작은 가정의 곱으로 쪼개면 몇 분 안에 규모를 알 수 있고, 그 가정이 다음에 확인할 것을 알려 준다.
misconception: 정확한 데이터가 없으면 시장 규모를 판단할 수 없으니, 남이 말한 숫자를 믿거나 조사부터 해야 한다.

sources.text: 문제 쪼개기와 페르미 추정(어림 계산)의 일반적인 방법
모든 인구, 비율, 잔 수는 설명용 가상 가정이며 실제 조사 자료가 아님

factChecks.note: 도시 추정 계산: 500,000명 × 0.8(성인) = 400,000명, × 0.5(매일 커피 마시는 비율 가정) = 200,000명, × 2잔 = 400,000잔, × 1/4(밖에서 사는 비율 가정) = 100,000잔. 모든 비율은 가정이며 실제 통계로 제시하지 않았습니다.
집주인의 '하루 100만 잔'은 추정치의 10배입니다. 1,000,000 ÷ 100,000 = 10. 카드에서는 '모든 가정이 동시에 크게 낮아야 가능하다'고만 표현했습니다.
매장 앞 추정: 아침 통행 3,000명 × 1/20 = 150잔. 손익분기 250잔(가정)을 넘으려면 3,000 ÷ 250 = 12, 즉 12명 중 1명이 사야 합니다.

cards.title: How many coffees does your city drink a day?
body: Mia runs a busy café and is looking at a second site. The landlord leans in: "This city drinks a million coffees a day. You can't miss."
Mia has no market report. She has a pen, a napkin and ten minutes before the next viewing. That turns out to be enough to check the claim.

image.label: A café owner doing math on a napkin next to a coffee cup
image.brief: 카페 테이블 위 냅킨에 손으로 쓴 곱셈 나무(사람 수 → 비율 → 잔 수). 옆에 커피 한 잔과 펜. 배경 창밖으로 도시 거리. 실제 브랜드 로고나 컵 상표는 넣지 않음.

cards.title: Where should Mia start?
body: She wants to know if a million coffees a day is believable for a city of about 500,000 people. What's the best first move?

options.text: Search online for "coffee consumption per city"
options.feedback: Fast if a good source exists, but most figures mix home and café coffee, or cover a whole country. She'd get a number without knowing if it fits her question.

options.text: Split it: people, share who drink coffee, cups each, share bought outside
options.feedback: This is **breaking the problem into parts**. Each piece is something she can guess sensibly, and the pieces multiply into an answer.

options.text: Take her own café's daily sales and multiply by the number of cafés
options.feedback: It uses real data, which is good. But her busy café is not an average café, so the total could be far too high.

cards.title: Four guesses, multiplied.
body: Every number here is an assumption, not a fact. The point is that each one is easy to question. Result: about **100,000 cups** sold a day, not a million.

breakdown.label: Cups bought outside
breakdown.detail: Guess: 1 in 4, the rest at home or work

cards.title: Rough is good enough here.
body: This is **estimating with rough numbers**. Mia doesn't need the exact answer. She needs the size: tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, or millions.
Any single guess could be off. But for a million café cups to be true, her guesses would all have to be far too low at the same time. The landlord's number now looks like a sales line, not a fact.

image.label: Three bins labeled tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands, millions
image.brief: 크기가 다른 상자 세 개: "10,000s", "100,000s", "1,000,000s". 추정치 공 하나가 가운데 상자 근처에 들어가고, 맨 오른쪽 상자에 집주인의 말풍선 "1 million!"이 붙어 있음. 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: Which number does her decision actually need?
body: The city total is interesting. But Mia is deciding about one shop on one street.

options.text: A sharper estimate of the city's daily total
options.feedback: More precision on the wrong question. A city of 100,000 daily cups can still have a dead street.

options.text: Cups she could sell at this site on a weekday morning
options.feedback: This is **defining the problem first**. The real question is whether this spot can cover its costs, so that's the number to estimate.

options.text: How many cafés already operate in the city
options.feedback: Useful context on competition, but it doesn't tell her how many people walk past this door.

cards.title: The estimate points to what to check.
body: Mia breaks the new question down: about 3,000 people pass the site each morning (a guess), and maybe 1 in 20 buys a coffee. That's **150 cups**. She thinks she needs about 250 to break even.
To reach 250, 1 in 12 passers-by would have to buy. So the weakest guess is foot traffic. She spends one morning outside with a clicker. One cheap count now beats a year of rent.

image.label: A person counting passers-by outside an empty shopfront
image.brief: 빈 상가 앞 인도에 서서 카운터기(클리커)를 누르는 사람. 출근길 사람들이 지나가고, 상가 유리창에 'For lease' 표지(실제 부동산 회사 로고 없음). 아침 햇살.

cards.title: An estimate is only as honest as its assumptions.
body: Rough numbers size a decision. They don't replace checking the one assumption the decision hangs on.
Write every guess down where others can see it. Hidden assumptions can be bent until the answer says what you hoped, which is exactly what the landlord's million did.
cards.softwareNote: Software founders face this in market sizing. "1% of a billion-dollar market" hides every assumption. Instead multiply: businesses with the problem × share who'd pay × price, then test the shakiest number with real sales calls.

cards.title: Now it's a paper-cup wholesaler.
body: You distribute supplies to cafés in your region. A maker offers a new compostable cup, with a big minimum order. Before committing, you want a rough sense of demand. Which estimate fits?

options.text: Cafés you serve × cups each uses a day × share likely to switch
options.feedback: The problem is defined as *your* demand, and it's broken into parts you can guess or ask about. The switch rate is the number to test with a few customers.

options.text: People in the region × coffees per person per day
options.feedback: A fine rough estimate, but of the wrong thing. It counts every cup, not the cups your customers would buy from you.

options.text: Use the maker's own sales forecast for your region
options.feedback: Quick, but the maker wants a big order. You'd be borrowing someone else's assumptions without seeing them.

cards.title: Big unknown numbers are just small guesses multiplied.
body: Three ideas from this unit did the work:
list: **Define the problem first:** estimate the number your decision needs
**Break it into parts:** turn one unknown into a few guessable pieces
**Estimate with rough numbers:** aim for the right size, then check the weakest guess
cards.callout: **Try it today:** estimate how many customers could reach your business each week. Write four guesses, multiply, and circle the one you'd check first.
